newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Astra sees sharply higher net in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Astra sees sharply higher net in 1997.

text.p: Indonesia's largest automobile manufacturer, PT Astra International, said on Wednesday it expected to post a net profit of 627 billion rupiah (US$258 million) in 1997, up from 470 billion rupiah in 1996.

"We expect to book a net profit of 627 billion rupiah in 1997 as demand for our new Kijang van and Honda motorcycle is sharply higher," Rini Suwandi, the company's finance director, told reporters after an annual meeting of shareholders.
Last January, she said Astra expected to book a net profit of 614 billion rupiah for 1997.
In the meeting, the company received shareholder approval to split the nominal value of its stock from 1,000 rupiah to 500 rupiah.
Suwandi said the firm expected sales of the Honda motorcyle to reach one million units by the end of 1997.
In 1996, Astra sold 654,262 units of Honda motorcycles, up 37.2 percent from 476,721 units in 1995. Total sales of all brands of motorcycles in 1996 was 1,377,206 units.

Astra's president commisioner Muhammad "Bob" Hasan said the company's car sales experienced a downturn in the first nine months of 1996 after the government announced its controversial national car policy, which gives tax and tariff benefits to a company controlled by President Suharto's youngest son to make cars in association with South Korea's Kia Motors.
The benefits allow the national car, called Timor, to be sold at a substantial discount to other vehicles.

However, Astra's car sales rebounded during the last quarter of 1996 and a strong performance was expected in 1997, Hasan said. Analysts have said the Timor has not fared well in the market despite its lower prices.

The total number of cars sold by Astra came down to 160,563 units in 1996, from 206,833 units in 1995. As a consequence, Astra's market share declined from 54.6 percent in 1995 to 48.4 percent in 1996, the company said.
"The downtrend is normal as we also introduced a new model of Kijang van in the market. So there was a downtrend as buyers shifted to a new model," Hasan said.

He said the new model had received a good response from the market. "Buyers have to wait until September 1997 to purchase a new Kijang as Astra production cannot meet the demand," he said without giving further details.
Hasan declined to comment on a possible cut in car prices following fierce competition and a recent move by conglomerate Bimantara, controlled by another son of Suharto, to cut prices of its sedans.
Both of Bimantara's sedans are locally produced in association with South Korea's Hyundai Motor Co.

"We have to discuss it with our marketing department. But cutting sale prices is not the simplest way to compete. There are a lot of factors that we have to learn before we can cut prices," he said, adding that after-sales services and availability of spare parts in the market were also important factors.

Hasan, who is a close associate of Suharto and took control of the company after a takeover battle last year, emphasised that Astra was ready to face competition despite a government decision to order state institutions to buy the Timor car.
"We are not worried with the policy to make Timor an official car for government. We believe demand in our market is so huge," he said.

Suwandi said the company planned to float three of its subsidiaries. The banking and plantations units would be listed on the exchange in September and October this year while the auto parts subsidiary would be floated in February 1998, she said.
